CCAR-P · DOMAIN D4 · 16% · ~10 QUESTIONS

Evaluation, Testing and Optimization

This domain tests one thing: can you run a production Claude system like an engineer instead of a demo builder? That means measuring quality before and after every change, catching the failure that aggregate numbers hide, choosing the right test for the right risk, and trading cost, latency and quality against each other on purpose. Every question here is scenario based. The traps punish vibes and reward evidence.

0. The eval flywheel: why evaluation comes first

Evaluation (eval) means scoring your system on a fixed set of test cases so you can compare versions. An eval is not a demo. A demo shows what the system can do once. An eval shows what it does every time, on cases you chose in advance.

Here is the core mental model of this whole domain. Production LLM work is a loop: ship a change, measure it against a fixed test set, diagnose the failures, fix them, measure again. Without the fixed test set, every iteration is a guess. You cannot tell whether a new prompt helped or hurt, because each conversation you eyeball is a different sample. Evals turn opinions into numbers.

This matters for the exam because almost every D4 question is secretly a question about this loop. Should the team go live? Run the eval. Which of two prompts is better? Run the eval. Did the new model version break anything? Run the regression eval. The correct answer is almost never "trust the demo" or "eyeball a few examples".

Common misunderstanding "Evals are a pre-launch checkbox." No. Evals run before launch (to decide if you are ready), after every change (to catch regressions), and continuously in production (to catch drift as data and models change). A team that evals once has a snapshot. A team that evals always has a steering wheel.
Scenario shape: a team argues about whether a new prompt is better, each side showing hand picked examples. The credited answer is the one that proposes a fixed eval set and compares both versions on it. The trap answers are "ship the one the senior engineer prefers" and "eyeball more examples".

Exam relevance: this loop is the frame for every other section. When a question asks what to do first, the answer is usually "measure": define metrics, build the eval, then decide.

1. Defining metrics: measure what the task actually needs

A metric is a number you compute the same way every time, so versions of your system can be compared fairly. Defining metrics is the first official objective, and it is where most real projects go wrong: they pick a metric that is easy to compute instead of one that matches the task.

The five metric families

The exam blueprint names five families: accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security. A production system usually needs at least one from each.

  • Accuracy (quality). Did the output do the job right? The exact formula depends on the task (see the table below). Never assume one formula fits all.
  • Latency (speed). How long from request to usable response. Report percentiles, not averages: p50 is the median (half of requests are faster), p95 means 95 percent of requests finish within this time, p99 is the worst realistic case. Users feel the p95, not the mean. Averages hide the slow tail.
  • Cost. Tokens in, tokens out, tool calls, judge calls. Usually expressed per request or per thousand requests. Cost is a first class metric because LLM bills scale with usage, and a quality win that triples cost can still be a bad decision.
  • Safety. Rate of harmful, biased or disallowed outputs: refusal rate on attacks, toxicity scores, bias across demographic groups. Measured on adversarial test sets, not normal traffic.
  • Security. Rate of prompt injection success, data exfiltration attempts blocked, PII (personally identifiable information) leaked. Like safety, measured with attack style test cases.

Match the metric to the task

Precision is: of everything the system flagged, how many were correct. Recall is: of everything it should have flagged, how many did it catch. F1 is the harmonic mean of the two, a single number that punishes a system that is great at one and terrible at the other.

Task typeRight metricWhy
Classification (spam or not, contract type)Precision and recall per class, F1Plain accuracy hides class imbalance (see the worked example below)
Extraction (dates, amounts, names)Field level exact match or F1One wrong field can void a contract, so partial credit must be strict
Open generation (summaries, drafts)Rubric scored by LLM judge or humans (1 to 5 per criterion)No single right answer exists, so you score dimensions like completeness and faithfulness
Agentic task (multi step tool use)Task success rate, steps to completion, tool error rateA correct final answer reached in 40 wasteful steps is a different system than one that does it in 6
Latency sensitive (chat, voice)p50 and p95 time to first token and total timeStreaming means the first token matters separately from the full answer

Worked example: the trap of aggregate accuracy

This is the single most tested idea in D4, and it appears almost verbatim in community exam reports. A contract review assistant must reach at least 95 percent accuracy on each of five contract types. On a 1,000 contract eval set it scores 96 percent overall. The team wants to go live. Should they?

Do the arithmetic on a concrete case. The set holds 200 contracts of each of the five types, and the system scores: Employment 98, NDA 99, Lease 97, Vendor 96, Privacy 90 percent. Correct answers: 196 + 198 + 194 + 192 + 180 = 960 out of 1000, which is 96 percent overall. The overall number passes. The Privacy segment at 90 percent fails the 95 percent bar. One in ten privacy contracts is reviewed wrong, and the average hides it completely. That is the whole trap in one paragraph.

The fix is segmented (sliced) metrics: compute every metric per contract type, per language, per customer tier, per input length, whatever dimensions matter. The launch gate becomes "every segment passes", not "the average passes".

Common misunderstanding "High accuracy means the model is good." Accuracy is a property of the system on a specific test set, not a property of the model. The same model scores differently on different segments, different prompt versions and different judges. Always ask: accuracy of what, on which data, measured how.
Guardrail metrics When you optimize one metric, name the metrics that must not regress. These are guardrail metrics: safety rate, p95 latency, cost per request. An A/B test (section 4) ships only if the primary metric improves AND every guardrail holds. Exam questions love asking what to monitor alongside an optimization: the answer is the guardrails, not just the thing you improved.
Scenario shape: a target like "95% accuracy on each of five document types" plus an overall number that looks passing. The trap answers: go live on the aggregate, switch to a bigger model, add more training data. The credited answer: measure per segment, fix the failing segments first. A second shape: pick the right metric for the task (precision vs recall for a fraud detector where missing fraud costs more than false alarms: recall matters more).

Exam relevance: metric definition is the foundation every other objective builds on. Expect 2 to 3 questions where the right move is choosing or slicing a metric before acting.

2. Eval datasets and test frameworks: mixed methods

Golden dataset: a fixed set of inputs with known good answers, curated by hand, that every version of your system is tested against. Regression suite: the subset you run after every change to prove nothing that used to work broke. A golden dataset is the asset; the regression suite is how you use it daily.

Building the dataset

Start from production reality, not imagination. Sample real user inputs, anonymize them, and have domain experts write or verify the expected answers. Aim for coverage across the segments from section 1: every contract type, every language, short and long inputs, easy and adversarial cases. A few hundred well chosen cases beat ten thousand near duplicates.

Three hygiene rules:

  • Label quality beats size. One wrong expected answer poisons every comparison. Have a second person spot check labels, and track inter-rater agreement (do two labelers agree? If not, the task definition is fuzzy, not the labelers).
  • Keep a held-out split. Never tune prompts against the full set. Tune on a dev split, report on a held-out test split. Otherwise you are grading your own homework: the prompt overfits the test cases and the score lies.
  • Version the dataset. When you add cases, bump the version and keep the old one. If scores jump between versions, you need to know whether the system improved or the test got easier.

Mixed methodologies: three layers

No single scoring method fits every case. Production evals layer three methods, cheapest first:

  1. Deterministic (rule based) checks. Exact match, regex, JSON schema validation, "did it call the right tool with valid arguments". Fast, free, zero judgment calls. Use for everything checkable by code.
  2. LLM-as-judge. A separate model scores outputs against a rubric (section 3). Handles open ended quality that rules cannot, at a fraction of human cost.
  3. Human review. Slow, expensive, and the gold standard for taste, nuance and high stakes calls. Reserve for sampled audits, judge calibration and launch gates.

The pattern: rules catch the obvious, the judge scores the bulk, humans audit the sample. Most traffic never reaches a human, but the human layer keeps the other two honest.

The test framework around the dataset

A dataset alone is a spreadsheet. A test framework is the harness that runs it: it feeds each input to the system, captures outputs plus traces, scores them with the layered methods above, stores results per version, and diffs versions side by side. The framework properties the exam cares about:

  • Determinism where possible. Pin model versions and seeds for eval runs, because a moving model makes before/after comparisons meaningless.
  • Side by side diffs. For each case, show old output vs new output with the score delta. Engineers diagnose from diffs, not from averages.
  • Failure bucketing. Group failures by type (wrong tool, invented fact, format break) so a 2 percent regression becomes an actionable list.
  • CI integration. The regression suite runs on every prompt or code change, like unit tests. A change that drops the score blocks the merge.
Common misunderstanding "Our eval set is our training data, so more overlap is fine." Contamination (test cases leaking into prompts, few shot examples or fine tuning data) inflates scores and hides real weakness. Keep few shot examples and test cases strictly separate. If a case appears in the prompt, it cannot also be in the test.
You might be wondering: how big should the golden set be?

Big enough that a real regression moves the number, small enough to run fast. A practical rule: start with 200 to 500 cases covering every segment. Then do the statistics. If your system scores 90 percent on 200 cases, the 95 percent confidence interval is roughly plus or minus 4 points, so only swings bigger than that are trustworthy. If you need to detect a 2 point change, you need roughly 1,000 cases. The exam will not ask you to compute this, but it will reward answers that mention statistical power when someone proposes A/B testing on 50 samples.

Scenario shape: a team with no evals, or evals built from the same examples used in the prompt. The credited move: build a golden set from sampled production traffic with human verified labels, keep a held-out split, layer rule checks plus judge plus human audit. The trap: "add more few shot examples from the test set" (contamination) or "just run it on 20 examples the engineer wrote" (unrepresentative).

Exam relevance: dataset design questions test judgment under constraints: representativeness, label quality, held-out splits, and mixing methods by cost. Look for the answer that balances all four.

3. LLM-as-judge: a powerful grader you must not trust blindly

LLM-as-judge means using one language model to grade another model's output. You give the judge the input, the output, and a rubric (a scoring guide), and it returns a score plus reasoning. It exists because human grading does not scale: a judge can score ten thousand summaries overnight for dollars, where humans would take weeks.

How it works under the hood

A judge call is a structured prompt, not magic. The recipe:

  1. Give the rubric as criteria with anchors. Not "rate quality 1 to 5" but "5: every claim in the summary appears in the source; 3: one unsupported claim; 1: contradicts the source". Anchors (concrete descriptions per score) are what make judges consistent.
  2. Ask for verdict plus reasoning. Reasoning first, then the score: models score more reliably when they explain before deciding.
  3. Pin temperature to 0. Temperature controls randomness: 0 means the most likely token every time (deterministic), higher means more creative sampling. A judge must be deterministic, so temperature 0.
  4. Parse the score as structured output. Force JSON with a schema so "4" never arrives as "four-ish".

The failure modes (the exam loves these)

A judge is a model, so it has model biases. Know all four by name:

  • Self preference. A judge tends to score outputs from its own model family higher. Fix: judge with a different model family than the one you are evaluating, or at least blind the judge to which system produced the output.
  • Verbosity bias. Judges reward longer answers even when the extra words add nothing. Fix: add "prefer concise correct answers" to the rubric, or normalize by length.
  • Position bias. When comparing A vs B, judges favor whichever comes first (or second, depending on the model). Fix: run both orders and average, or score each output independently instead of pairwise.
  • Drift and inconsistency. The same judge scores differently after a model version update, and disagrees with itself on reruns. Fix: pin the judge model version, rerun a calibration sample regularly, and never compare scores across judge versions.

Calibration: proving the judge agrees with humans

Calibration means checking the judge against human graders on a shared sample and measuring agreement. A judge is only as good as its agreement with the humans it stands in for.

The procedure: take 100 to 200 outputs, have humans score them with the same rubric, have the judge score them, then compute agreement. The standard number is Cohen's kappa, which measures agreement beyond chance: above 0.8 is strong, 0.6 to 0.8 is acceptable for most uses, below 0.6 means the rubric or the judge needs work. Recalibrate on a fresh sample whenever the judge model, the rubric or the data distribution changes.

One more rule the exam tests: the judge must never be the system under test grading itself without blinding. "We used the same model to generate and judge, and it says we are great" is a finding of nothing.

Common misunderstanding "The judge gave us 4.6 out of 5, so quality is 4.6." A judge score is not an absolute truth. It is a proxy with known biases, meaningful only for comparing versions scored by the same judge, same rubric, same model version. Treat judge scores as relative (A beats B), never as absolute (A is excellent).
Scenario shape: scores improved after the team switched the judge to the same model that generates the answers (trap: celebrate; credited: self preference, re judge blinded or with a different family). Or: the judge prefers the longer of two equal answers (verbosity bias, fix the rubric). Or: scores shifted after a judge model upgrade with no product change (drift, pin versions and recalibrate). Learn to match each symptom to its bias and fix.

Exam relevance: LLM-as-judge questions test whether you know its failure modes and the calibration discipline. If an option says "trust the judge", it is wrong. If it says "calibrate against humans and pin the version", it is probably right.

4. A/B testing and iterative improvement

A/B test: split live traffic randomly between the current system (A, the control) and a changed version (B, the variant), then compare them on the same metrics. It exists because offline evals cannot capture everything: real user behavior, real input distributions, and real business outcomes only appear in production.

Designing the test

  1. One change at a time. If B differs from A in prompt, model and retrieval settings, a win tells you nothing about what worked. Change one variable per test.
  2. Pick the randomization unit. Usually the user or the session, not the request: if one user sees A on one message and B on the next, the experience is inconsistent and the data is polluted. Hash the user ID into a bucket and keep them there for the whole test. This is called sticky bucketing.
  3. Name the primary metric and the guardrails up front. Primary: the thing you hope improves (task success rate). Guardrails: the things that must not regress (safety refusal rate, p95 latency, cost per session). Writing these down before the test prevents cherry picking the metric that happened to win afterward.
  4. Size it for the effect you care about. Small traffic or a tiny expected gain means a long test. A test that is too short produces noise, not answers. As a rule of thumb, you need enough samples that the observed difference would rarely happen by chance. If traffic is thin, prefer offline evals and reserve A/B for big changes.
  5. Run it long enough to cover weekly patterns. Weekday and weekend users differ. A three day test can mislead; one to two full weeks is the norm for user facing systems.

LLM specific wrinkles

  • Non determinism. The same prompt can produce different outputs across calls. This adds noise, so LLM A/B tests need more traffic than a button color test. Lower the temperature or average multiple samples when noise threatens the read.
  • Judge consistency. If a judge scores the arms, it must be the same judge, same version, same rubric for both. A judge change mid test invalidates the comparison (drift, from section 3).
  • Novelty effects. Users react to "new", not to "better", in the first days. Do not call a test on the first 48 hours.
  • Carryover. If the variant changes conversation memory or cached state, users crossing between arms contaminate results. Sticky bucketing plus clean state per arm fixes this.

The iteration loop

A/B testing is not one test. It is the loop from section 0 at production scale: form a hypothesis ("a shorter system prompt cuts latency without hurting quality"), ship the variant to a slice of traffic, read primary plus guardrails, then promote, kill or iterate. Keep a log of every test with its hypothesis and outcome. Teams that do not write down hypotheses repeat failed experiments; the log is organizational memory.

One caution: peeking (checking results daily and stopping the moment B looks good) inflates false wins. Decide the runtime or the sample target in advance and respect it. If you must peek, use sequential testing methods designed for it, which the exam will not ask you to compute but may ask you to name as the fix.

Common misunderstanding "The B arm won on quality, so we ship it." Not until the guardrails clear. A variant that answers better but leaks PII (personally identifiable information) twice as often, or costs three times more per session, fails the test. The credited exam answer almost always checks the guardrails before promoting.
Scenario shape: a team ran an A/B test for two days on 200 users and wants to ship (trap: ship; credited: insufficient sample and runtime, extend or fall back to offline evals). Or: B wins on the primary metric but p95 latency doubled (trap: ship on the win; credited: guardrail tripped, reject or optimize first). Or: users saw both variants across messages (trap: ignore; credited: randomization unit should be the user with sticky bucketing).

Exam relevance: A/B questions reward process discipline: one variable, pre registered primary and guardrail metrics, sticky randomization, adequate runtime, no peeking. The wrong answers rush.

5. Diagnosing system issues: hallucination vs prompt failure vs model mismatch

When a Claude system produces bad output, the fix depends on the cause, and the causes need different medicine. The exam names three: prompt failure, hallucination, and model mismatch. Learn to tell them apart by their signatures.

Hallucination: the model states as fact something false or unverifiable, with full confidence. It is not lying; it is predicting plausible sounding text without grounding.

Prompt failure: the model misunderstands or ignores your instructions: wrong format, skipped steps, answered a different question. The capability is there; the directions were unclear, contradictory or buried.

Model mismatch: the task exceeds what the chosen model can do: multi hop reasoning it fumbles, a language it barely knows, context longer than it handles well. The prompt is fine; the engine is too small for the hill.

Signature symptoms

SymptomLikely causeConfirming test
Confident false facts, invented citations, wrong numbers that look rightHallucinationGive the model the source text and ask it to quote: if the answer changes, it was ungrounded
Right content, wrong format; skipped required steps; answered a different questionPrompt failureRewrite the instruction to be explicit and test again: if the behavior flips, the prompt was the bug
Reasoning collapses on hard cases, works on easy ones; long context questions degradeModel mismatchRun the same prompt on a larger model: if it now works, the small model was the ceiling
Good answers sometimes, bad answers other times, same inputNon determinism or flaky toolRun the same input 10 times at temperature 0: variance points at the model, consistent failure points at the prompt
Worked last month, fails now, nothing changed on your sideModel version drift or data driftCheck the provider changelog and rerun the regression suite (section 2)

The diagnosis procedure

  1. Reproduce it. Capture the exact input, model version, prompt version and seed. If you cannot reproduce it, you cannot prove you fixed it.
  2. Isolate the layer. A Claude system has layers: retrieval, prompt, model, tools, post processing. Test each alone. Swap in known good retrieved docs: if the answer fixes itself, retrieval was the fault, not the model.
  3. Change one thing. Same discipline as A/B testing. If you rewrite the prompt AND switch models, you learn nothing.
  4. Check the trace. Read the full trace (section 7): what did the model actually see? Truncated context, a failed tool call hidden by a retry, or a system prompt that got overridden are all visible in traces and invisible in the final answer.
Common misunderstanding "Bad output means we need a better model." Model upgrades are the most expensive fix and they do not cure prompt failures or ungrounded generation. Diagnose first: most production issues are prompt or retrieval problems wearing a model costume. The exam punishes "throw a bigger model at it" as a first resort.
You might be wondering: what about tool failures?

Tool failures deserve their own bucket. Signatures: the model calls the wrong tool, passes invalid arguments, or ignores a tool result. Causes split the same three ways: the tool description was unclear (prompt failure, fix the description and add examples), the arguments were invented (grounding, validate with schemas), or the task needs planning the model cannot do (mismatch, decompose into smaller steps). Always validate tool arguments against a schema before executing: it turns silent corruption into loud, diagnosable errors.

Scenario shape: a symptom description plus four candidate fixes. Match symptom to cause to fix: invented facts need grounding (retrieval, citations), ignored instructions need prompt repair, hard reasoning failures need a stronger model or decomposition. The traps are cross column fixes, especially "upgrade the model" for what is clearly a prompt or retrieval problem, and "rewrite the prompt" for what is clearly beyond the model's capability.

Exam relevance: diagnosis questions test the triage discipline: reproduce, isolate the layer, change one thing, read the trace. The credited answer names the cause before the cure.

6. Token, latency and cost optimization

Every production Claude system lives inside a triangle: quality, latency, cost. Push one corner and the others move. The architect's job is not to minimize cost or maximize quality in isolation. It is to pick the point on the triangle the business asked for, and to know the price of moving.

Start with the vocabulary. A token is the unit the API bills and the model reads: roughly 3 to 4 characters of English per token. Input tokens are what you send (system prompt, documents, history). Output tokens are what the model writes, and they cost more per token and take longer, because generation is sequential: each token waits for the previous one.

Prompt caching: the highest leverage optimization

Prompt caching lets you mark a prefix of your prompt (system instructions, reference documents) as cacheable. The provider stores its processed form and reuses it across requests instead of recomputing it every time. It exists because most production prompts repeat a large static prefix with a small changing suffix.

The economics, from published Anthropic pricing. These are the numbers to memorize:

  • Cache write: 1.25 times the base input token price. You pay a 25 percent premium once to store the prefix.
  • Cache read (hit): 0.1 times the base input price. Ten times cheaper than normal input tokens.
  • TTL (time to live): how long the cache entry survives unused. Default 5 minutes; a 1 hour option exists at 2x the base input price for cache writes (versus 1.25x at the 5-minute TTL). TTL is the expiry timer: touch the entry with a matching prefix and the timer resets.

The critical constraint: caching works on exact prefix matches. If request A starts with [system + doc1 + doc2] and request B starts with [system + doc2 + doc1], the prefixes differ and nothing is reused. Order your prompt with the most static content first and the most variable content last, or caching silently does nothing.

Worked example with real arithmetic

A support assistant sends a 10,000 token product manual with every request, plus 500 tokens of conversation. It serves 100 requests per hour. Base input price: $3 per million tokens (illustrative published tier).

  • No cache: 100 requests times 10,500 tokens = 1,050,000 tokens. Cost: 1.05 x $3 = $3.15 per hour.
  • With cache: one write of 10,000 tokens at 1.25x = 12,500 token equivalents = $0.0375. Then 99 requests hit the cache: 99 x 10,000 tokens at 0.1x = 99,000 token equivalents = $0.297. The 500 variable tokens per request are never cached: 100 x 500 = 50,000 tokens = $0.15. Total: 0.0375 + 0.297 + 0.15 = $0.48 per hour.

Same answers, 85 percent cheaper. The break even is after a single reuse of the prefix within the TTL window: the 25 percent write premium is repaid by the first cache hit, which saves 90 percent of the prefix's input price. If the prefix is never reused before the TTL expires, the 25 percent write premium is wasted.

The rest of the optimization toolkit

  • Model routing. Send easy requests to a small fast model (Haiku class) and hard ones to a large model (Sonnet or Opus class). A classifier or a rule (short question, no tools needed) does the routing. Typical split: 70 to 80 percent of traffic is easy, so routing cuts the bill by half or more while the hard cases keep top quality. The exam trap: routing everything to the biggest model "for quality" with no cost analysis.
  • Batching. The Batch API processes non urgent requests at roughly half price with up to 24 hour turnaround. If the use case tolerates delay (nightly report generation, bulk classification), batching is the cheapest per token option. Never batch user facing chat.
  • Context compaction. Long conversations grow the input every turn. Summarize older turns into a compact state and drop the raw history. This cuts tokens per request and often improves quality, because the model stops drowning in stale context.
  • Output discipline. Output tokens cost more and stream slower. Ask for exactly what you need: "answer in under 100 words" or structured JSON instead of prose. Verbose defaults are a silent budget leak.
  • Right size retrieval. In RAG, retrieving 20 chunks when 5 suffice multiplies input tokens. Tune chunk count on the eval set: quality first, then cut until quality moves.
The optimization order When a scenario asks how to cut cost, apply optimizations in this order: 1) prompt caching (near free if prefixes repeat), 2) output discipline and retrieval right sizing (quality neutral), 3) model routing (small quality risk, big savings), 4) batching for delay tolerant work, 5) model downgrade as a last resort, validated on evals. Each step gets re measured on the eval set before the next. The exam rewards this sequence and punishes jumping to step 5.
Common misunderstanding "Optimization means using the cheapest model." Cost optimization means the best quality per dollar at the required latency. Sometimes that is a bigger model with caching and short outputs beating a small model that needs three retries to get it right. Retries are the hidden cost multiplier: a cheap model with a 30 percent retry rate can cost more than an expensive model that nails it first try.
Scenario shape: a bill that is too high, or a latency budget that is blown. The credited answer picks the optimization that fits the constraint: caching when prefixes repeat (check the trap: unique prefixes per request), routing when traffic splits easy and hard, batching when delay is tolerated, compaction when conversations grow. A second shape: compute which option is cheaper from token counts. Show the arithmetic, not the vibe.

Exam relevance: expect numbers. Know cache write 1.25x and read 0.1x, batching around half price, and the prefix match rule. The traps test whether you check the precondition before applying the optimization.

7. Observability and monitoring: seeing the system in production

Observability means you can answer "what happened and why" for any request, from data you collected in advance. Logging records events; observability is the ability to reconstruct the full story of a request: what the model saw, what it called, how long each step took, what it cost, and where it went wrong.

Trace structure: the unit of understanding

Trace: the complete record of one request, organized as a tree of spans. A span is one timed operation: the top span is the whole request, child spans are the model call, each tool call, each retrieval step. Spans nest, so you can see that the 8 second request spent 7 seconds inside one slow tool call.

Every span should carry the same core fields:

  • Timing: start, end, duration. This is how you find the slow step.
  • Identity: model name and version, prompt template version, request and session IDs. Without versions, you cannot compare before and after.
  • Usage: input tokens, output tokens, cache hits. Tokens convert directly to cost.
  • Outcome: stop reason, tool called with arguments, error codes, judge or rubric scores when available.
  • Content pointers, not content: a hash of the prompt, not the prompt itself when it contains user data. You need reproducibility without storing secrets.

PII redaction and log hygiene

PII (personally identifiable information): any data that identifies a person: names, emails, account numbers, health details. Redaction: removing or masking PII before logs are stored or shipped.

Rules that show up on the exam:

  • Redact at collection, not at query time. Once raw PII sits in a log store, every person with log access can read it, and every breach includes it. Strip it in the logging pipeline before storage.
  • Redact prompts, completions and tool arguments. All three can carry PII. A common pattern: store the trace structure plus hashes, keep full content only in a short lived, access controlled debug store with explicit retention.
  • Watch for PII in model outputs too. A model that echoes a customer's account number into its answer puts PII in your logs through the completion path.
  • Set retention windows. Debug traces with content: days. Aggregated metrics: months or years. The exam likes the principle of least retention: keep sensitive data only as long as its purpose needs.

From traces to monitoring

Traces answer "what happened in this request". Monitoring answers "is the system healthy right now". Build it in three layers:

  1. Dashboards: live views of the metric families from section 1: quality scores, p50 and p95 latency, cost per request, safety refusal rates, error rates. Segmented, always (section 1's lesson applies to dashboards too).
  2. Alerts: thresholds on the dashboards with owners. Alert on symptom, not cause: "p95 latency above 4 seconds for 10 minutes" pages someone; "quality score dropped 5 points week over week" opens an investigation. Alert fatigue is real: every alert must have a runbook entry saying what to do.
  3. Production evals: the loop never stops. Sample live traffic, score it with the judge plus human audit (sections 2 and 3), and watch for drift: quality decaying as user behavior shifts or the model version changes under you. A sudden quality drop with no code change on your side points at provider side drift: check the model version in your traces first.

Sampling: you cannot keep everything

Full tracing of every request is expensive and often unnecessary. Sampling means keeping a fraction of traces in full detail:

  • Head based: decide at request start (keep 1 in 100). Cheap, but you miss rare failures.
  • Tail based: decide after seeing the outcome (keep all errors and slow requests, sample the successes). Best signal per dollar: you always capture the interesting cases.
  • Always keep aggregates. Even unsampled requests contribute to counters and histograms, so dashboards stay complete while detailed traces stay affordable.
Common misunderstanding "Monitoring is watching a dashboard." Dashboards without alerts are television. Alerts without runbooks are noise. Production evals without a feedback loop are trivia. The exam's credited answers always close the loop: detect, alert, diagnose from traces, fix, verify on the eval set.
Scenario shape: "quality dropped in production, what do you check first?" The credited path: dashboards segmented by version and segment, then traces of failing requests, then the eval suite to confirm. The traps: retrain or switch models immediately (no diagnosis), or log full user prompts to debug (PII violation). A second shape: design logging for a regulated use case. The credited answer redacts PII at collection, keeps versioned traces, and sets short retention on content.

Exam relevance: observability questions test the logging contract: what each span carries, what gets redacted and when, and how traces feed dashboards, alerts and production evals. "Log everything including user data" is always wrong.

Exam checklist: D4 in one page

Read this last, the night before. If every line below feels obvious, you are ready.

  • Metrics: match the metric to the task (precision/recall per class, rubric scores for generation, task success for agents). Report latency as p50/p95, never just the mean. Name guardrail metrics for every optimization.
  • The segment trap: an overall number never satisfies a per segment bar. Always slice metrics by the dimensions the requirement names. 96% overall with a failing segment means do not ship.
  • Datasets: golden sets from sampled production traffic, human verified labels, held-out split, versioned. Never tune on the test split; never let test cases leak into prompts.
  • Mixed methods: rule checks for everything checkable, LLM judge for the bulk, human review for sampled audits and calibration. Layer by cost.
  • LLM-as-judge: rubric with anchors, temperature 0, structured output. Four biases: self preference, verbosity, position, drift. Calibrate against humans (kappa above ~0.6), pin the judge version, blind the judge.
  • A/B tests: one variable, sticky per user randomization, pre registered primary plus guardrail metrics, enough runtime to cover weekly patterns, no peeking. B ships only if it wins and no guardrail trips.
  • Diagnosis: invented facts need grounding (retrieval, citations). Missed instructions need prompt repair. Hard reasoning failures need a bigger model or decomposition. Reproduce, isolate the layer, change one thing, read the trace.
  • Cost: cache write 1.25x, cache read 0.1x, exact prefix match required, static content first. Optimization order: caching, output discipline, retrieval sizing, model routing, batching for delay tolerant work, downgrade last with evals.
  • Observability: traces as nested spans with timing, versions, tokens, cost, outcomes. Redact PII at collection. Dashboards segmented, alerts with runbooks, production evals watching for drift. Tail based sampling for signal per dollar.

Across all of D4, the exam rewards one instinct above all: measure before you act, and distrust the single number. The wrong answers ship on vibes, optimize blindly, or trust an uncalibrated judge. The right answers define the metric, slice it, test the change, check the guardrails, and only then decide.
